Seltzer is simply plain water into which carbon dioxide (CO₂) gas has been dissolved under pressure. That dissolved gas is what creates the bubbles you see — and the fizzy, tingly feeling you experience when you drink it. It goes by other names too: carbonated water, sparkling water, or fizzy water.

That's really the whole secret: take ordinary still water, pump CO₂ into it at high pressure, and you get seltzer.

When the bottle or can is sealed, the CO₂ stays dissolved in the water because of the pressure inside. The moment you open the container, the pressure drops, and the gas starts escaping from the water in the form of bubbles. This is the same reason a shaken soda bottle fizzes explosively when opened — the gas wants out.

Pure seltzer tastes almost like water, but not quite. Because CO₂ dissolves in water, it forms a weak acid called carbonic acid. This gives seltzer a very mild, clean sharpness — almost like a gentle bite — that plain water simply doesn't have. Many people describe it as "refreshing" or "crisp." The carbonation also creates a light, tingly sensation on your tongue and in your throat as the bubbles pop.

It is not sweet, not salty, and not bitter in its pure form. If seltzer tastes like anything beyond water, it's really just that slight, pleasing sharpness from the carbonation.
How is seltzer different from similar drinks?

This is where many people get confused, so it's worth being precise:

Seltzer vs. club soda: Club soda is also carbonated water, but it has minerals added to it — things like sodium bicarbonate or potassium sulfate. These minerals give club soda a faintly salty or mineral-ish taste. Pure seltzer has nothing added — just water and CO₂. This is the key distinction.

Seltzer vs. sparkling mineral water (like Perrier or San Pellegrino): Sparkling mineral water comes from a natural underground spring and contains minerals that occur there naturally. These minerals give it a distinctive, complex taste. Seltzer, by contrast, is made artificially — regular water is simply carbonated mechanically. It has no special minerals.

Seltzer vs. tonic water: Tonic water is carbonated, but it contains quinine (a bitter compound) and sugar or sweeteners. It's noticeably bitter and sweet. Seltzer has none of that — it's neutral.

Seltzer vs. soda/soft drinks: Sodas like cola or lemon-lime drinks are carbonated water loaded with sugar, flavoring, coloring, and other additives. Seltzer is just water and CO₂ — nothing more (in its basic form).

The simplest way to remember it: seltzer is the purest, most stripped-down form of sparkling water — no minerals, no sweeteners, no flavors added.

Today, seltzer is very commonly sold in flavored versions — such as lemon, lime, grapefruit, berry, or mango. These flavored seltzers have natural flavors lightly infused into them. Crucially, they still contain no sugar or sweeteners — the flavor is usually quite subtle, more of a hint than a strong taste. Popular brands of flavored seltzer include LaCroix, Bubly, and Spindrift.

Flavored seltzer should not be confused with flavored sodas, which are sweet. Flavored seltzer is not sweet — it just smells and tastes faintly of the fruit.

You will often hear the term "hard seltzer." This is seltzer water that has alcohol added to it — typically around 5% alcohol by volume (similar to a beer). Hard seltzers are usually also lightly flavored. They became very popular in the late 2010s and 2020s. Brands like White Claw and Truly are well-known examples. If you see the word "hard" in front of seltzer, it means it contains alcohol.

• Drunk on its own, as a refreshing, calorie-free alternative to still water. Many people prefer the fizz, especially with meals.
  • As a mixer in alcoholic drinks — for example, mixed with whiskey or vodka, or added to wine to make a spritzer.
  • In mocktails and cocktails, where the bubbles add lightness and texture.
  • Mixed with juice — for example, mixing seltzer with a splash of orange juice gives a light, fizzy drink without the heaviness of a full soda.
One important note about the word
"Seltzer" and "seltzer water" mean exactly the same thing — people use both. You will often see it written either way. The word "seltzer" on its own already implies water.

Seltzer is water made fizzy by dissolving carbon dioxide gas into it — with absolutely nothing else added — giving it a light, clean, slightly sharp taste and a characteristic tingly feeling when you drink it.
